title: Olokun
imageAlt: Olokun standing with a trident amid a sweeping ring of water
imageCaption: Olokun — protector, sailor, and Rahu adventurer.
dek: A social, deeply attached protector forced to discover what love is allowed to do—and whether care can remain care when fear wants control.

facts.Status: Alive after the October mist expedition; resumes care for the company after the rescue (19 October 2026 UTC source posts).

body:
Olokun’s philosophy begins as sociability, not doctrine. He jokes, sails, competes, arm-wrestles, encourages strangers, and becomes part of communities quickly. People become important to him; shared history makes them harder to abandon; responsibility follows. His development runs from belonging → attachment → conflicting loyalties → principle → triage and loss → death → return.

Core proposition: differences in strength, knowledge, authority, and capability are real. Ownership does not follow from them. One may volunteer oneself; love or power does not automatically grant the right to spend another person.

2024 · the person before the principle

A 10 July chronicle calls him “Optimistic Olokun”: cheerful, courageous, kind, and already beloved around Pristinia, with victories in Oiche Arena and an arm-wrestling contest. On 23 June, however, his engagement with a creature in a burned forest accidentally freed a minion associated with Death. Early Olo acts inside uncertainty; sometimes that helps, and sometimes it makes the world worse.

His first explicit boundary arrives in an ordinary dispute on 12 July, when Grokthar keeps pressing after a rejected challenge.

I told you no pana. When a man says no, is no. Accept my rejection.Olokun

The scene does not make him a fully formed philosopher. It plants the question that later scales upward: what does strength, love, fear, knowledge, or authority permit one person to do to another?

30 July 2024 · fear, the Gate, and Arjahn

Olo is frightened by the Gate’s sea or pool aspect, yet he steadies Arjahn by asking him to think of the people they can help and the family they can honor. His courage is behavioral, not an absence of fear. That early care later becomes causal history: after Olo gives Arjahn the Scepter of Faith, Arjahn will use that same gift to return him from death.

September 2024 · belonging without surrendered conscience

Becoming Rahu gives Olo power, knowledge, secrecy, obligations, and relationships with Ephraith, Dasa, and others. Only weeks later, a Delerium secret pits his oath against his friends. He wants them to find the answer but refuses simply to hand it over.

I want you guys to find the answer, I just don’t want to tell you myself.Olokun

He neither declares the oath meaningless nor treats friendship as irrelevant. His discomfort with the Dasa life-force system makes the same point: he can belong to a people without surrendering judgment to them. Papirak becomes “sweet gramps,” an example of Olo’s habit of accumulating family through repeated presence rather than blood.

30 December 2024 · the Warden

The Warden pursues Olo relentlessly. His attacks initially achieve little, though a strike against its blue clock-heart interrupts it; allies heal, hasten, reposition, and rescue him. His refusal to let Death take him again preserves an essential truth: survival matters to him. Later self-risk is not indifference to living.

2025 · Aria becomes a person without becoming safe

Olo’s history with Aria moves through hostility → repeated contact → personalization → understanding → attachment → continued moral disagreement. Scribonia’s imprisonment in a gemstone keeps her harm concrete. The bath, teasing, attraction, a kiss, dance, and vulnerability let Olo see the frightened “small child” beneath Pride without erasing the ruler capable of coercion and cruelty.

On 10 October, Aria invites him to help raise humanity high enough to reshape the world. Olo refuses to spend Zarathians in a celestial war. Both want people to be safe, but disagree over who may authorize the cost of that war.

27 September 2025 · a mortal answer to divine failure

After hearing of divine war and a damaged creation, Olo refuses the conclusion that failed caretakers make the world worthless.

World is good. The people that live it, they make it good, not only gods.Olokun

This is not naïveté. He has already seen dead Gael and answers that friends remain there healing it. Mortals participate in what makes creation worth continuing even when gods conceal history, make mistakes, and leave others living with the consequences.

5 October 2025 · leadership as stopping

When Arandiel wants to continue through exhaustion and loss, Olo argues that Zarathis will lose important leaders if they push on. He says there is no glory in pointless death, calls for rest, and offers to keep watch himself. His strongest leadership often restrains escalation: protection before glory.

17 October 2025 · Aionia and the world map

Olo tells Eugene that time travel with Aionia let the group obtain a world map and overhear younger Cala and Nuru discussing the Gate and Papirak’s Wish. He remembers the gods acknowledging fault and insisting adventurers must never know. Direct evidence of divine concealment deepens his skepticism without making Aria’s war automatically right. The group uses access to history to gain knowledge, not to treat past lives as editable material.

The War Council · whose sacrifice?

Aria says pain must sometimes be endured for victory. Olo answers with the compressed form of his mature ethic:

My pain. Not everyone’s.Olokun

Both want safety and both will fight. Aria increasingly accepts suffering imposed on others for the future she considers necessary. Olo insists that willingness to suffer does not confer the right to volunteer everyone else.

6 November 2025 · unfinished grief and the protector’s manifesto

Talan kills Aria unexpectedly, leaving no final reconciliation and no clean proof that either of them won the argument. When Death appears for her body, Olo rebukes allies for treating wounded enemies as disposable, insists that the purpose of killing and dying is protection, and asks Death what he actually wants.

His speech reveals both virtue and danger. He continues seeing people inside enemies and monsters. Yet “If we could have saved them all, we would! We should have!” turns every unsaved person into a possible personal failure. Refusing to abandon anyone can slide into believing he must prevent every loss.

January 2026 · choice, death, and return

During the Abyss or Kurayami confrontation, Olo must choose between Wren and Aravil. He chooses Wren; Aravil is taken as a trophy. The archive does not declare the choice correct. It is triage, and it destroys the fantasy that enough care can always save everyone.

The Abyss commands “Olokun. Die.” Olo dies. Arjahn then resurrects him with the Scepter of Faith that Olo had once given him. The causal chain matters: gift → relationship → retained object → death → another person’s choice → return. Resurrection does not erase Aravil, the decision, or the terror. It proves that Olo’s own survival can depend on having empowered someone else.

March–May 2026 · fear survives resurrection

In a March retreat involving worms, Olo supports the right to withdraw but lashes out at Arjahn from fear, then continues mapping and practical work. He returns with resolve, not purification. By May, Babel-Ashur confronts him with exhausted defenders, a losing Vanguard, fallen friends, and the question of how many people anyone can remain responsible for.

Papirak’s death and the Luminar expedition

News of Papirak’s death hits Olo as the loss of “sweet gramps” and as proof that Magnus continues acting unchecked. Olo carries useful older history about Papirak, Wish, and divine intervention into the expedition, but his recollection that the relevant knowledge was erased is corrected by Scribonia: it was locked away and wrapped in madness.

The correction clarifies rather than diminishes Olo’s role. He increasingly functions as a carrier of lived history whose memories remain most reliable when compared with witnesses and records at the point where exact magical mechanics matter. During the reversed-gravity accident, he is caught by the altered field and must accept help escaping it.

The mature distinctions

  • Power is not permission. Capability does not settle moral authority.
  • Love is not ownership. Wrath, Aria, and Death all show that sincere attachment can coexist with terrible control.
  • Understanding is not obedience. A wound can deserve understanding without gaining the right to command.
  • Belonging is not surrendered conscience. Rahu, friends, Aria, Pristinia, and the wider world create obligations that no single loyalty erases.
  • Strength exists to protect. Violence is instrumental, never the measure of victory by itself.

Where the virtue breaks

Olo can move from “I cannot abandon people” to “I am responsible for preventing their loss,” and from there to “I may need to stop them from making dangerous choices.” His continuing test is whether he can protect people without deciding that loving them gives him authority over choices that remain theirs.

The open record

Important gaps remain: his exact arrival and earliest sailing, Rahu initiation ritual, relationships with Ephraith, Dasa, Sophina, and Anky, the original transfer of the Scepter, the full Aria chronology, the Void expedition, precise world-map alteration mechanics, the complete Wren–Aravil choice, and his later Babel-Ashur history. The archive will not turn those gaps into certainty.

The painter reaches the people

Olokun’s attempts to communicate through paintings become consequential when a blood-painted warning leads the party toward Babel’s captives. He presses the group to stop delaying and follows the trail into the caves. During the rescue he draws the executioner’s attention away from the people and continues fighting with his friends’ support.

Afterward a nomad asks whether he is the painter. Olokun confirms it and promises safety, while acknowledging that the adventurers have arrived too late for some. At the refuge he listens to the survivors’ stories. Communication has become a responsibility toward living people, rather than simply a way to map an unfamiliar island.

A first astral reconnaissance from the castle

With Elenia watching his body at the castle, Olokun projects into a star-filled, weightless space connected to his body by a silver cord. He sees a terrifying distant creature and what may be a gate or land, but turns back without reaching it. He re-enters his body safely. His hope of becoming a courier remains an ambition: no destination or safe inter-island route is established. When he describes matching the strongest people of his village, he hopes his father would be proud and thanks Elenia for bringing him back to life.

Learning without agreement

In the castle’s January discussions, Olokun hopes that joining the Emerald Veil could help him bring knowledge and assistance to Prima and Gael. His pragmatism has an uncomfortable edge: he asks Adelia to conceal her worship for the greater good, while acknowledging that they cannot force her. The exchange preserves a disagreement between friends, rather than a shared rejection of the gods.

Stone, water and a difficult reconciliation

Fenwae, a Silver Star stone mason, shows Olokun a marble quarry and an unfinished dam intended to collect drinking water. The narrator describes well-fed workers, clean air and blocks moved by magic and engineering. Fenwae says the Verdant Circle has advised maintaining river flow; the exchange does not establish a completed dam or measured ecological recovery. Their conversation turns to the dispute over Aria: Olokun explains why the adventurers felt betrayed, while Fenwae describes how the accusations looked to her own people. They leave with a better understanding of the disagreement, not a definitive verdict on the battle.

Scene evidence: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

Organization as a form of protection

While working near the walls, Olokun argues that the settlements need more organization and should prioritize infrastructure and economy. Alyhotep describes the pressure arrivals put on resources and the effort to make residents more self-sufficient. This is a shared civic discussion, not an enacted policy.

Scene evidence: 1, 2.

October · fear finds another route through care

Olokun gathers the expedition, welcomes Wren back and guides Ryvyt, who is new to this part of Babel. In the jungle a giant blind salamander paralyzes and badly wounds him. Ryvyt heals him and removes the paralysis; Olokun eventually lands the final blow. His embarrassment is his response to needing help, rather than evidence that the company considers him a failure.

After Arjahn cuts his tether, Olokun enters the mist tied to Nymera and Ryvyt. He sees his father telling him that Oya has contracted his old disease. Convinced his sister needs him, he cuts his own rope and mistakes his companions for threats. Nymera tries to carry him out, but her own vision interrupts the rescue. The apparent father vanishes and Olokun is left paralyzed, crying and blaming himself. The scene does not establish that Oya has actually become ill.

Released by the clearing, he helps gather the group, thanks Ryvyt and tries to reassure Nymera. He refuses Death’s offer even when Oya’s safety is used as an inducement. His answer returns to an earlier commitment: the people of the world, rather than obedience to its gods, are why he fights. After the vision he checks on his friends and helps arrange Scribonia’s return to the refuge. Fear has exposed his vulnerability without removing his capacity for care.

Early October · company beyond the fighting

Before a hunt, Olokun notices Scribonia’s weariness and reassures Nymera. He proposes the outing and a visit to the coast afterward, leaving room for companionship rather than demanding an immediate cure for grief.

After the spiders are defeated, he uses a stone-like healing item to close the company’s wounds. They reach the shore where the first arrivals landed. Olokun splashes Scribonia with shaped water, trying to give his friend a brief release from the war. Scribonia lets the water reach him. The small gesture does not settle his losses, but shows care persisting outside a crisis.

Scenes in sequence

Selected scenes follow choices, knowledge and consequences. Dates identify UTC source postings; this October session was played on 18 October in New York.

  1. 2026-10-02 · quest

    Care leaves room for a pause

    Olokun checks on his companions, heals the hunting party and takes them to the coast, where he playfully splashes Scribonia.

    Known at this stage
    His friend names weariness that ordinary rest cannot remove.
    Consequence
    The company makes room for more than preparation for the next battle.
    Still unresolved
    The pause does not establish a completed emotional recovery.

    Receipt 1 · Receipt 2 · Receipt 3 · Receipt 4 · Receipt 5 · Receipt 6

  2. 2026-10-19 · quest

    The protector also needs a rescuer

    Paralyzed and badly wounded by the salamander, Olokun depends on Ryvyt’s healing and restoration before helping kill it.

    Known at this stage
    The jungle remains dangerous beyond the increasingly safe refuge.
    Consequence
    His survival depends on another companion’s preparation and action.
    Still unresolved
    His embarrassment is not a narrator judgment of his worth or ability.

    Receipt 1 · Receipt 2 · Receipt 3 · Receipt 4 · Receipt 5 · Receipt 6 · Receipt 7 · Receipt 8

  3. 2026-10-19 · quest

    Oya’s apparent danger and an offer refused

    The mist lures Olokun with an apparent illness threatening Oya. After release, he refuses Death’s offer involving her safety.

    Known at this stage
    The visions have made rescuers look like monsters and driven him to cut his tether.
    Consequence
    He returns to protecting companions without accepting the threatened bargain.
    Still unresolved
    Oya’s illness, Death’s protective promises and his claims about Aria remain unconfirmed.

brief.basis: Existing public dossier, explicit status facts and named timeline participants. Selected events are a reading guide, not a complete list or a ranking of importance.

relationshipMap.title: Olokun’s relationship web
relationshipMap.intro: Olokun becomes philosophical because people matter to him first. Select a relationship to trace belonging, attachment, conflicting loyalties, triage, loss, death, and the continuing test of protection without ownership.

nodes.title: Aria / Pride
nodes.subtitle: Enemy, person, attachment
nodes.history: Their history moves from hostility through repeated contact, teasing, attraction, dance, vulnerability, and attachment. Olo sees the frightened person beneath Pride without forgetting her coercion and cruelty.
nodes.consequence: Their central disagreement concerns sacrifice: Aria accepts suffering imposed for the future she wants; Olo answers, ‘My pain. Not everyone’s.’ Her death leaves both grief and argument unfinished.
nodes.evidence: The relationship arc and disagreement are established; parts of the chronology remain incomplete.

nodes.title: Arjahn
nodes.subtitle: Gift returned as life
nodes.history: Olo gives Arjahn the Scepter of Faith. After Abyss commands Olo to die, Arjahn uses that retained gift to resurrect him.
nodes.consequence: The causal chain—gift, relationship, death, another person’s choice, return—proves that survival can depend on having empowered somebody else. Later fear still makes Olo lash out at Arjahn.
nodes.evidence: Gift and resurrection are established; the original transfer’s full context remains incomplete.

nodes.title: The Rahu
nodes.subtitle: Belonging with retained conscience
nodes.history: Becoming Rahu gives Olo power, knowledge, obligations, and relationships. A protected Delerium truth immediately places his oath against his desire to help friends discover the answer.
nodes.consequence: He refuses both easy betrayal and surrendered judgment. Belonging becomes morally serious precisely because it does not erase other loyalties.
nodes.evidence: Initiation and oath consequences are established; many individual Rahu relationships remain incomplete.

nodes.title: Wren
nodes.subtitle: The person he chose
nodes.relation: Triage without a clean moral victory
nodes.history: In the Abyss confrontation, Olo must choose between Wren and Aravil. He chooses Wren; the archive refuses to declare the choice correct merely because she survives.
nodes.consequence: The decision destroys the fantasy that care and strength can always save everyone. Wren’s survival remains bound to the person not chosen.
nodes.evidence: The choice is established; its full circumstances and later relational aftermath remain incomplete.

nodes.title: Aravil
nodes.subtitle: The person he could not save
nodes.history: When Olo chooses Wren, Aravil is taken as a trophy. His later death and return do not retroactively make the original triage harmless or inevitable.
nodes.consequence: Aravil becomes the enduring cost inside Olo’s protector identity: a person he loved did not become less real because the choice was impossible.
nodes.evidence: The taking is established; the full choice mechanics and later reconciliation remain open.

nodes.title: Kurayami / Abyss
nodes.subtitle: Power that commands death
nodes.history: After forcing the Wren–Aravil choice, Abyss commands, ‘Olokun. Die.’ Olo dies. The act is domination in its most compressed form: another will treats his life as an executable instruction.
nodes.consequence: Resurrection answers the command without erasing its terror or the choice preceding it. Olo returns because another relationship intervenes.
nodes.evidence: The command, death, and resurrection are established; parts of the confrontation remain unrecovered.

nodes.title: Papirak
nodes.subtitle: Sweet gramps and living history
nodes.history: Olo calls Papirak ‘sweet gramps’ and carries memories of Papirak, Wish, and divine intervention into later expeditions. Papirak is both beloved person and irreplaceable historical witness.
nodes.consequence: His death becomes grief and an archival crisis. Olo’s recollection remains valuable even where Scribonia must correct the exact magical mechanism.
nodes.evidence: The affection and remembered history are established; Olo’s account is not treated as mechanically infallible.

nodes.title: Magnus Niriin
nodes.subtitle: Danger without disposability
nodes.history: Olo distrusts Magnus and recognizes the danger around him, yet resists the conclusion that a misguided person may simply be discarded or killed once inconvenient.
nodes.consequence: His position keeps judgment from becoming dehumanization. It also tests whether refusing to abandon someone can become another attempt to control them.
nodes.evidence: Olokun’s stated position is established; later trust remains unresolved.

nodes.title: Gartina
nodes.subtitle: Coffee, tactics, grief
nodes.history: Gartina prepares coffee specifically for Olo and remembers the tactical patterns surrounding danger to him. Her later self-blame shows how deeply his survival mattered.
nodes.consequence: The relationship joins small attentions to an impossible question: whether anyone can prepare well enough to guarantee that another person returns.
nodes.evidence: The care and later guilt are established; the full chronology remains incomplete.

nodes.title: Elenia
nodes.subtitle: Standing together through exile
nodes.history: During the 22 December verdict, Olo stands with Elenia while Magnus and Adelia support exile. He then leaves Zarathis with her and Aravil through the Shining Shores.
nodes.consequence: The act makes loyalty political without erasing disagreement. Their departure preserves companionship while accepting that the region’s judgment has material force.
nodes.evidence: The vote and departure are established; the broader friendship remains incompletely documented.

profile.personality: Olokun is curious, socially generous, and morally stubborn about consent. He makes mistakes—sometimes enormous ones—but his strongest principle is that protection belongs to people rather than institutions, gods, or the glory of a cause.
profile.achievements: He explores ruins, seas, dungeons, Rehevä, Voraketh, and Babel-Ashur; helps de-escalate conflict; survives the Abyss; and returns when Arjahn uses the Scepter of Faith he had earlier given away. He also refuses Death’s logic at the war council and repeatedly argues against abandoning the misguided as disposable. Toured Fenwae’s quarry and unfinished dam, then discussed how the dispute over Aria looked to both the adventurers and the Zarathians.
profile.relationships: Arjahn’s friendship carries anger, resurrection, and repair through shared mapping. Wren is the person Olo chooses under impossible pressure; Aravil is the loss inside that choice; Scribonia challenges and sharpens his thinking; and his arguments with Aria make his phrase “My pain. Not everyone’s” part of the world’s moral vocabulary.
